utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good morning, everybody. Good morning for Dr. Cehajic. We may continue immediately. Please take the floor. Sometimes it's better to know in which case we are, so it should be called. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Nicholas Koumjian with Ann Sutherland, assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic, John Ostojic and Mr. Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we can really start.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the usher please move the ELMO machine a little to the left, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, before we broke yesterday, we were talking about staff at the hospital. Can you tell me how many staff were there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before these events, I believe that there were between 550 and 580 employees.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Of that number, approximately what percentage were of Bosniak ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, I don't think I'm able to tell you what the exact percentage was. My best estimate would be 40 per cent, 30 to 40 per cent. I do not know the exact data.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And approximately how many per cent would have been of Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A small percentage, because there were not more than 16 per cent of Croats living in Prijedor. So the percentage of Croats employed at the hospital was not as significant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is it safe to say that the remaining percentage were persons of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and others who declare themselves as members of some other ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Of the number of persons that you have said worked at the Prijedor hospital, do you know approximately how many persons of Bosniak ethnicity were doctors or professional staff?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either, I'm afraid, this other percentage, but in view of the overall composition, in any case, it would be a smaller number than the Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit -- it was numbered 465 in the Rule 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, could you please read the title of the document.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "General Hospital, Prijedor. List of employees whose employment has been terminated." Do you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many names appear on that list?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you please tell me the signature block at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Director of the hospital, Dr. Radojka Elenkov, specialist of internal medicine."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Next to each name, a date appears. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you please peruse that list and tell me from your knowledge those persons that you believe are of Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Topic, Jelena, listed under number 11. Karacic, Dr. Mario, listed under number 20. 22, Grozdanic, Josipa, I think. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, before you go on, can you just tell me, Jelena Topic at number 11, do you know what her occupation was?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was a nurse, a head nurse in the psychiatry department.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And number 20, Dr. Mario Karacic?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a doctor, a surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And number 22, Josipa Grozdanic?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about her. I don't know what her occupation was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you continue?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Sikora, Zeljko, a Croat, number 47.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was that the doctor that you mentioned yesterday as an internist?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He was an intern undergoing specialisation at the gynecology department. I may have mentioned him having been at the police station together with my husband. I think I said that my husband told me that he was there as well. Juric, Ana.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is she listed at 103?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, number 103.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And where did she work?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was an administrative assistant. She worked in an office. Zec Dubravka, 111.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And her occupation?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was a biochemist. She worked at the laboratory. This is so far as this list is concerned. There may be other persons whose ethnic background I am not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On that list, can you give me the number of any person of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 19, for instance, Dr. Risto Stojanovski. He's a Macedonian, probably an orthodox by religion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What department did he work in?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at the time he was away on specialisation, but I'm not sure. I know that he was not at the hospital at that time. He was undergoing some sort of training outside our institution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do any Serb -- persons of Serb ethnicity appear on the list that you know of?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 38, Nukic Slavica. I know her, but she is married to a Muslim. She is a Serb but married to a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What department did she work in?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She worked at the laboratory. She was a lab worker. Listed under number 50, there's Vukotic Dzusanka. She could be Serb, but I don't know her. Judging by her name, she may be a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know the person listed at number 98?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Zoran Vikalo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What department did he work in?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also away undergoing specialisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The person listed at number 85, do you know that person's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 85, I didn't notice Emilija Jordan, but I think she is a Ukrainian of Catholic religion. She worked in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The other names that appear on the list, are they persons of Bosniak ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain with respect to the majority of these people, but in respect of some of them, I'm not quite sure. There was another individual whom I saw on the list, but I don't know what his ethnic background is, so I wouldn't discuss him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: From that list, how many persons are there that you know of that are deceased or missing, and can you please list their name and number and their occupation?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kadiric Ratib, under number 1, he was an ambulance driver. He drove the hospital ambulance. I'm sure that he is missing. I know this from his family. And I also know that he's listed in the book of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you speak with members of his family?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with some of them. Not with his wife, but with his relatives who know that he is missing, that he disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you can go to the next name but state the number first, and then the name, please.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 11 -- I'm sorry, no, 12: Turkanovic, Fikret, under number 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an engineer, and he was with the technical department. He was actually the head of the technical department of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How have you come to know whether he's deceased or missing?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From his relatives, and also from the book of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just in relation to numbers 1 and 12 that you've mentioned, were you told when they died or when they went missing?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't specifically gather this type of information. I just learned whether they are alive or not, but what actually happened, when they died or when they went missing, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 43, Hamulic, Razim. He was a medical technician working at the surgery department. He's no longer amongst the living. His wife is working at the same institution where I am currently working. She is an assistant, dentist assistant, and she was the one who told me her husband disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 46, Dr. Esad Sadikovic. He was an ear, nose, throat doctor; he was the head of the department. And I saw in the book of the missing persons that he is missing. I have never met any of his relatives, so I was unable to hear anything from his family.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 47, Dr. Zeljko Sikora. As I already said, he was undergoing specialisation at the gynecology department. His name can also be found in the book of missing persons, and at the time I was living -- while I was in Zagreb, 1994, I saw his mother on several occasions. She was hoping that he was alive, but he hasn't turned up since.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 55, Adnan Ekinovic. He was an x-ray machine technician, senior technician, with the diagnostics department. He has been found, that is, his body has been found in the Hrastova Glavica mass grave near Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 56, Islam Bahonjic, also an x-ray machine technician with the diagnostics department. When I went to the identification procedure, I saw his documents also at Hrastova Glavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about others. In respect of some of them, I'm sure that they are alive, but in respect of others, I'm not sure. I couldn't tell you anything else about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know the names of other people not on that list that you know are either deceased or missing? And can you please tell me their names, what their occupation was, and how you know that they are either deceased or missing?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about my colleagues, because I inquired with other doctors, so I know who is missing. I have already mentioned Dr. Esad Sadikovic, Dr. Sikora, Dr. Osman Mahmuljin, an internal medicine specialist. And Doctor -- and a psychiatrist, Dr. Rasim Music, and a surgeon, Dr. Begic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I can just interrupt you. How do you know that Dr. Osman Mahmuljin, the internal medicine specialist, how do you know he is either deceased or missing?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name can be found in the book of the missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Dr. Rasim Music?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Dr. Rasim Music, I have had contact with his family. He has two brothers who are alive, so they told me about him. And his name can also be found in this book. As for Dr. Begic, I only saw his name in the book of missing persons. I didn't have an opportunity to inquire about him with his family. Dr. Jusuf Pasic, also in the book of missing persons. Dr. Suljanovic also in the book of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me. Sorry, also in relation to Dr. Jusuf Pasic, where did he work?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked in Kozarac. I don't remember exactly how old he was. He was probably born in 1935 or thereabouts. When he started working in Kozarac, I was still not a physician. I have known him personally for a very long time as a physician who worked in Kozarac. He never left Kozarac. I believe that he spent his entire career in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you speak with anyone in relation to him?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. He has a wife and two children, but they no longer live in the same area as I do. I didn't have an opportunity to speak about him with his family.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where did Dr. Suljanovic work, what department?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked in various surgeries in Prijedor. I do not know, but I think in the town of Prijedor. I do not know exactly in which one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Please continue of other names of persons that were colleagues of yours from the hospital or Mladen Stojanovic Medical Centre that you know are deceased or missing?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have mentioned those that I knew, and I think that I have mentioned them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know a Dr. Kemal Ceric?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I forgot to say Kemal, Dr. Kemal Ceric. I forget to mention him when I was talking about the doctors, and Seric Nedzad, who was the president of the court in Prijedor, Nedzad Seric.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In what department did Kemal Ceric work?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a microbiologist, and he worked in the lab of microbiology.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How do you know that he is deceased or missing?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke with his wife. I met her after the war, and she told me that he was missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also mentioned Nedzad Seric, the president of the court in Prijedor. How did you come to know of his fate?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also heard, and also from that book, it was listed there as a missing person. And I think in 1990 or 1993, I met his wife in Zagreb, and she was alone there and she told me that her husband was missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any other persons that are either deceased or missing from Prijedor town that you know of from speaking to family members?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My neighbour. He has been my neighbour, Mehmedagic, who was a lawyer, and he was a public defence lawyer, and a very dear person to me. And I think that he was very nice and generous person, and that he did his work in a very correct way in Prijedor, and people liked him a lot. And this is how I know from the book of the missing persons and what I heard from his wife who worked in the same hospital where I worked. She was a head nurse in the surgery department. Mehmedagic, Fatima is her name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know of any others?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There have been many, but maybe I should mention the husband of my sister, Kapetanovic, Mehmedalija. He was a professor. He had an MA in the biological sciences. Before the war, he had been a director what in Prijedor was called the "old hotel." It was the catering company. He was the director there before all the war events.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We will move on to another topic. In 1992, was any of your property taken?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They -- first they took my car. Some soldiers came to the house and they told me that I had to give the car to be used by the army. This was already in the first days, maybe in June, the beginning of June. At the very beginning, they took my car away.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did they give you a receipt?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't. They didn't give me any receipt, and I had problems afterwards because of that, because I thought that that was the way to maltreat me later on. Because they would come and ask for the car. Because they had come several times to ask for the car, and when I said that I didn't have the car, that I had given it away, then asked for the receipt. And when I told them I didn't have any receipt because I hadn't been given one, they were sending me to the military barracks to ask for the receipt, in order to be able to show it to them. And of course, I couldn't go there because I wasn't sure if I went -- had gone there, if I would ever return home. And that's why I waited for them to come without the receipt. I waited for those people who came for the car.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was your home ever searched?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did search it once, an official search, so to say. There were quite a few people. They were all dressed in military uniforms. They were policemen. There were several of them, and they searched the whole house. And they did not take anything from the house of my personal things at that moment, but they took all the documents that were there of my husband. He didn't even take -- he hadn't taken his ID with him. He didn't remember it. So all his documents were taken by these people, and all the photographs, my family photographs, so that all the pictures were taken from me. I asked them to leave the pictures of my children, that these were something for me to remember. But they didn't want to listen to me. They took everything. It was a sack of -- a bag of photographs. I had to give them the pictures, the photographs when my daughter graduated. So maybe it is not a big thing, not a very important thing in life, but for me, a part of my life has been erased because I don't have a photograph of my child when he was small. So this whole -- a whole part of my life was erased. This was a very difficult situation for me. I want to apologise because I'm crying, because you cannot compare this with what has happened, but this is also something that is important to many people, as it is important to me also.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you given any reasons as to why they were searching your apartment?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't give me any reasons. They didn't tell me why they were searching the house. I didn't know what they were looking for. They did not find anything, actually. And neither had they taken anything at that moment from my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many persons were there present conducting the search of your house?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several, but I know that in each room, there was one person, and that was about six or seven rooms which they had searched. And in each of these rooms there were some walking around in the hall, some were outdoors. So there was quite a number of people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned policemen and soldiers. How were the policemen dressed?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the police uniform which was actually -- it was a blue uniform, and on their arms, they had the signs of policemen. And the soldiers had uniforms, not camouflage uniforms, just the regular ones. I don't remember having seen any special signs. Maybe I didn't notice them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these people?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of those who I thought was a supervisor, he was a policeman. I don't know his name, but I knew him. He had been a policeman before, and then he was retired. And on that occasion, he had a police uniform on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you mistreated during the search?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not much. Some insults, that person -- that particular person told me, "What did you need that for, doctor, because you were the first lady of Prijedor? Why did you do that?" And I asked myself: What had I done? What was I accused of? And he was quiet for a while, and he said: "In the hospital, you cursed a Serb mother to the nurses." And I said: "No, I had never cursed because I was brought up in the family where there was no cursing, and I have never cursed, let alone somebody's Serbian mother. I wouldn't do that." He didn't comment any longer. And there were some other details. They asked me some questions, but they were not the things that should be mentioned. I think they were irrelevant -- they are irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was your home searched on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did come several times, but they didn't search the house but my garage, which the first time they had come, they saw what I had. So they looked for the following: They looked for the boat, motor boat. But I think they had an intention to treat me in a bad way rather than to take some things. And every time they came to the house, there were three or four of them. On one occasion, even five. And then I would take the key and I would go to the garage, because it was far away from the house because you have to pass two buildings in order to get to the garage. And I thought that they enjoyed the fact that I was ahead of him and that people were watching because some people were watching from the windows how I went in front of them to the -- to my garage. And then they would take what they wanted to or they didn't take what they didn't find, and this was some kind of a parade through that part of the city, of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were these people soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were -- every time, they were in military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did they take anything from the garage?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the second occasion, they took the boat and the engine of the boat, maybe some smaller things. I never checked. Because they asked for the engine, a motorbike of my son, but it was not there because I had given it to a neighbour. Immediately after they had come for the first time, I gave it to my neighbour, so they didn't find the motorbike but they were asking for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of your neighbour that you gave the motorbike to?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to move to another topic now. Did you attempt to speak to anyone in authority about your husband being detained in a camp?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did try, but I couldn't get to anyone. I tried to reach Dr. Kovacevic, and I thought that I was close to him. But at that moment, it didn't mean much. But I did have a feeling that I could find some understanding in him, but I wasn't able to get to him. I tried to reach him by telephone twice. Once, I went there. I went to the municipal building, but I could not reach them. So this attempt to reach this person or someone else was not successful.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you just pause there, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall between what time period this was?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been at the beginning of June when I tried and when I still thought something could be done. Later on, I was not even trying any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you said that you tried to reach "them," and you mentioned Dr. Kovacevic, who else were you trying to contact?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that I would contact Kovacevic and Dr. Stakic, because I thought that they were his co-workers at some point, and if I came, that I could reach Dr. Stakic also and ask him where my husband was. This, I thought, would be the most normal thing if I could come and ask whether I could do something. But of course, I was not able to do that, and I didn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you said that you attempted to reach them by telephone twice, do you recall what was -- who did you speak to when you telephoned?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time when I called, a secretary responded, and she said that they were not there. And since I hadn't expected, of course, they are not there, I thought neither of the two of them was there. So that telephone conversation ended in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the second occasion when I --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me. On that first occasion when you spoke to the secretary, did she tell you where they were?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked her where they were, where I could find them, and she said that they were in the Crisis Staff and that I couldn't reach them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On the second occasion, can you please tell the Court --

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She also told me that they were not there, and she -- that's what she told me, that she didn't know whether they would be there, something in that direction. So I didn't even try to call by telephone again because I knew that she would always tell me that they weren't there if they didn't want to let me come.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think you also said that you went to the municipal building on one occasion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. They said that they received the pay at the municipality, and my husband had this decision that he was on the annual leave and that that was the pay for that time. So I went to the municipal building to ask for the pay, not that I needed it, but in order for it to be a way to enter the municipal building if anybody asked me why I was -- why I had come. So I did enter the building, and in the hall, I came across Marija Mutic. She was an economist working in the municipality. I had known her for a long time. She was the best person of my sister at the wedding, and she greeted me. I told her why I was there. She said: "Don't go there. I shall go to the cashier." And when she came back, it was very difficult for her to tell me, but she said I wasn't able to get my husband's salary because whoever was in a camp was not allowed to receive his salary. This is what they had said. And then I asked if -- when I asked for Stakic and Kovacevic, she said they were not there, so I returned without having succeeded in anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your husband was the president of the Municipal Assembly, which was the highest organ in the municipality, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After your husband lost his job, do you know who took over as the highest authority in the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I now want to move to another topic. Were you in 1992 taken for questioning?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did take me for questioning. On the 11th of June, they came to my house to pick me up. There were three men, and they told me that I had to go for the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them, I didn't recognise him. I asked him on the way back what his name was. He said that he was a Montenegrin, Tajson. He had a T-shirt and trousers. The driver who drove us and the other person had some military uniforms on. I don't think they were marked with any special signs. The third person, I did not know, and who was left in my house when I had been taken. And the person who drove, the driver, I did know him. He was a boy from Prijedor. He was of the same age as my daughter, so I did know him, although he didn't say anything to me at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Pekija Drasko. He was the son of Pekija Petar, who used to work in the x-ray laboratory and who had been retired. When I started working as a young doctor, he already worked there as an x-ray technician.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were these men armed?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The didn't have rifles. They had guns, but they didn't have any rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My sister and I, because she was at my house, they took us both, and they drove us from Prijedor to -- this is Urije, is a part -- or a part of Prijedor, to the military barracks, which was in that part of the town. And I left the car with this person whose name was Tajson and took me throughout the barracks, both floors, which were both full of soldiers. They looked at me, but I was so scared that I couldn't even look. But they were watching us, and they didn't do anything. They just took me around, and we came back. He put me again into the car and drove me to the place where I was supposed to arrive, in some premises on the road to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the army barracks --

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, in Keraterm. It was around 15 minutes. He took me on both sides, and he was, like, looking for something. But he didn't say anything to anyone. And I concluded that he was not supposed to bring me there at all, but he only wanted to show me to those soldiers how he took the wife of the president of the municipality, or a doctor, how he was taking me around. Maybe it meant something to him. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you were taken to some premises on the road to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those premises...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those premises were -- was some administrative building of Keraterm which was on the right side of the road on the way to Banja Luka. And on the other side of that building, there was the Keraterm buildings and premises where the detainees were. I was not on that side. I was on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On the right-hand side of the road as you leave Prijedor, heading towards Kozarac, Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were you taken when you arrived at this building?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the first floor of that building. It was a long corridor and there were some people there, not many, but there were some people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you recognise anybody?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe there were other people which were familiar, but when I turned around, I recognised a man who -- maybe I wouldn't have recognised him, but he had some wounds on his face and on his nose, and there was some band-aid on his nose. But I still recognised him. It was Medunjanin Becir. He was a military administrator in Prijedor before those events, and I was afraid that maybe they had brought me because of him. I was afraid because of him, although I didn't know him very well. I maybe had seen him two or three times. I knew that -- I knew of him. I knew that he existed, but I didn't have any connection with him whatsoever. But I was afraid because this was just an accident that we were both there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned that he had a bandage on his face. What was -- in your opinion, what was his condition?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did have some bandage, and you can tell that everything was blue and swollen, the bandage and some cotton on his nose.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you or your sister recognise anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't recognise anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did your sister?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she didn't tell me about having met anyone whom she knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several rooms in this corridor and I could see people waiting in these rooms. I figured that those were interrogation rooms. And the one that I entered was a very simple room, with a desk and a chair in it. That was the room where I was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you know who was interrogating you?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I saw two persons, two interrogators whom I knew, in the corridor. But the one who interrogated me, no, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did the interrogation last?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It lasted from sometime just before noon until the evening hours, just before the curfew.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were you questioned about?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My feeling was that the interrogator himself didn't know what he was accusing me of, and it all boiled down to my having to say where the wife of Dr. Mujadzic was, Dr. Mirza Mujadzic's wife, who was the president of the SDA, and his wife was no longer in Prijedor. Among other things, he also me whether I knew anything about what my husband did, where he held meetings, what he had been preparing, and things like that. But the interrogation itself wasn't very insistent, neither concerning myself nor my husband. He just kept asking general questions as to who I was, but I could tell that he knew quite a lot. He also inquired about whether I had been a member of the communist league, whether I was still -- whether I was a member of any political party at the time. I said I was not. And I told him about my reasons why I was not a member of any political party, why I had been a member of the communist party, and so on and so forth. But he was not unpleasant and I think that, altogether, he treated me in a humane way. He asked me a number of questions. He didn't -- he was not accusing me of anything. Generally speaking, he was not unpleasant. I wish I knew his name. I wish I knew a name of the person who, despite his capacity, was not inhuman in his treatment of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you made to sign a statement?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. What he kept telling me was that if I didn't say anything about my husband, that I would remain there until I did so. And then I told him then it means that I will remain here forever because I have nothing to say about him. At one point in time, he cut the conversation short, and he said: "You better sign this document." And I said I didn't know where Mirza Mujadzic's wife was. I didn't know anything about her. I never socialised with her, nor was she ever my friend. So I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier Becir Medunjanin, and you said that he was a military administrator. Do you know what his exact position was prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had some sort of a function. I believe the title was called an officer in charge of military affairs with the Department of the Interior of the town of Prijedor, the Department of the Ministry of the Interior of the town of Prijedor. He may have been some sort of a chief. He was the number one in this department.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was this to do with the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened after your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My sister was afraid for me, and she told me that a group of soldiers had passed and climbed up the stairs. They appeared to have some knuckle dusters on their hands. She said they were metal and pointed. They ran into the room where Medunjanin was, whereas the interrogator who was there had left the office in the meantime to have some rest because my interrogator also would leave the office from time to time, and I would remain there alone. So she was very afraid when they entered the office, but they eventually came out of this office. The interrogator appeared after a while and he said that he could no longer conduct the interrogation because the man was unconscious. All of the people who were in the corridor were then taken downstairs, including my sister, but this is something that I was not aware of because I was inside. So I didn't experience this kind of fear. My sister told me that she was afraid that the group of soldiers would enter the office where I was, but nothing of the sort happened, and we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. returned home.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you report to work after your holiday leave had expired?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I tried to call to see what would happen with me. I was very much afraid at the time. I didn't feel like going to work, but if I had to, of course, I was ready to go to work. So I called them up and told them that my leave was coming to an end, and I asked them what to do. I called a person by the name of Radojka who at the time was the manager of the hospital department, the administrative manager of the hospital, and I told her what was happening. I told her that my leave was coming to an end and she said: "Well, you're not on leave. You have -- you are on the waiting list." And I said: "Well, what am I supposed to do? Shall I report later on?" And she said: "No, there's no need for you to report. If we need you, I will give you a call." And that was that. That was the end of our conversation. I never contacted her again, nor did I ever heard of her later on -- hear of her later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, this person that you spoke to by the name of Radojka, is this Dr. Elenkov --

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Dr. Radojka Elenkov.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... at the bottom of the document that you were shown?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that document hasn't been given an exhibit number. It was P465 in the Rule 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Normally, we do it at the end. Don't you intend to tender any other documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let's wait until the end. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, in 1992, was your son living outside Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. At the time, he was studying medicine in Zagreb and was not living in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was your daughter ever taken for questioning?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My daughter was in Prijedor. She was working as a general practitioner at the time at the local health centre. But she was also on standby at home. She was no longer working at the time. She did not receive any document whereby she would have been sacked, so it can be said that she was on standby. Her departure was a more tragic experience for me, although I don't remember its date. I remember the date of my departure. It was the 11th of June. It was the Bajram. I'm sorry, not departure, but the fact when they were taken. She was picked up in my apartment, although everybody knew that she was not living with me, that she was married and living outside my house. However, they came to fetch her in my apartment. I told him that she was not there. They asked me where she was. And I said that she was living in the vicinity of my block of flats some hundred metres away as the crow flies. But I didn't dare say that she was there because I was afraid that they would go there to get her and then that they would take my son-in-law. That was the reason why I called her on the telephone and told her that she should come to my place, that she was being asked for. She had a small child, and I said that if she had someone to leave the child with, to do so. If not, to come to my apartment without child. She eventually came without the child and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was she taken to the SUP for questioning? Was your daughter taken to the SUP for questioning?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she was taken to SUP, to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did her questioning last, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as long. It was -- it lasted for a couple of hours, not longer than that. Of course, it seemed like eternity to her, but it was a shorter interrogation than mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you at some point arrange for your daughter and other relatives to leave Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I realised that both of us were in danger, and I thought that it would be good for her to be sent somewhere. But we didn't dare leave together with other residents who were transported in buses or trucks and then taken to the central Bosnia and Zenica. I was trying to find some other way, secret way, for my daughter, her child, and two of my nieces to leave the town. My sister had two daughters; one was underage. And this is how I learned through the radio that there was a convoy leaving from Bosanski Novi organised by the United Nations, and that only those who already had tickets could join the convoy. There was another convoy that was supposed to leave before that one but didn't, so we were told that only those who had some kind of tickets were allowed to leave with that convoy. I tried to call a man whom I knew in my official capacity, he was the director of the pharmacy, and I thought that he might be willing to help my daughter join the convoy despite the fact that she didn't have the ticket. So I obtained his telephone number. I called him up. He was very forthcoming and friendly. And I said: "Do you remember me?" "Of course, madam, I remember you." And I said that I was asking for a favour. I said that it was about my child, not about myself. I asked for my daughter to be enabled to leave this -- to leave Prijedor through Bosanski Novi with this convoy, although she didn't have the ticket. He said that he was not aware of what is being organised, but that he would give me a call later. And maybe within one hour or so, he called me back. He said: "Let her come. Everything will be organised for her." And he gave me the name of a woman working in the municipality and whom I could contact to this respect. And she said that if there are any problems, that I should call him back, that he would do everything to enable her to leave. So my daughter, with her child, my sister with two daughters, left in this convoy. They said that they had reservations. They sat on the first seat of the bus of this convoy. But there were other people who had tickets and who had reservations and who were complaining about the fact that their seats had been taken. But this man said: "This is a doctor. She is a doctor. If there are any problems, she will be able to help you." And this is how they managed to cross the border on the 23rd of June and reached Croatia, where they were eventually met by my brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said the 23rd of June. Is that the correct date?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: July, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The other persons on this convoy, do you know what ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. But I guess that most of them were Muslims and Croats who wanted to leave Bosanski Novi, who had asked for this convoy to be organised for them. I don't think that they were Serbs, although it is possible that there may have been Serbs amongst them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to move to another topic now. Do you know a person by the name of Simo Miskovic?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. I knew him before, even before, at the time when he worked at the police before these events. He was retired, not because of his old age, but because of the nature of the service, it was possible for him to retire early.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did you known him prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember exactly when we met. I think that I had known him ever since I started working in Prijedor. He was married to a nurse who worked at the hospital. So on account of that, I probably saw him more often. But I'm sure that at least 10 or 15 years before the events.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was he a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know if he held any position within the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did. At one point in time, he was the president of the SDS. As I said, at one point in time -- I don't know exactly when this was, but I know from the media that he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to Simo Miskovic about your husband's whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I believe it took place in August. A lady acquaintance of mine of Serb ethnicity came to fetch me at my house, and she said: "Let's go have a walk." She used to be a student of my husband. And as we went for this walk, we were not very far from my buildings, some 100, 150 metres away. Simo Miskovic came by, and she greeted him. And I greeted him. He greeted me as well. So we stood there for a while. She tried to ask me what -- if he knew anything about my husband. She said: "Simo, do you know what happened to Professor Cehajic?" And he said: "Well, I don't know much. I know that he had been handed over to the military, the JNA. But that's all I know." Obviously, it was a very uncomfortable situation for him and he couldn't bear to look me in the eye. And my impression was that he was afraid to discuss the issue. It is possible that he already knew what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that he said that he had been -- your husband had been handed over to the military, to the JNA. Did Miskovic say who handed him over to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. He didn't tell me that, nor did I ask him any other questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did he say anything else?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. I don't remember that he said anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were the SDS offices in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were located in the block of flats where I lived, on the ground floor. The building itself had three entrances, and on the ground floor of the first entrance, the SDS had their premises before the events. I didn't see many people there, though I didn't really dare look around much or leave my apartment. But as far as I could observe, during that period of time, not many people gathered in these premises very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you spoke to Miskovic about your husband, how did you address him, in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not address him in any specific capacity. Well, he was just a member of a political party. I was not aware of any particular function that he had.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that he was president of the SDS. Do you know during which period this was?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know during which period this was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Dr. Milomir Stakic on the radio?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I did, though I must say I didn't pay much attention to that. But I remember that sometime in August, after the Omarska camp had been closed down, I heard a conversation. You see, there were many shortages, power shortages, at the time, so I didn't turn on the radio very often. But when I did, this was very traumatic for me so I avoided as much as possible listening to the radio. But on one occasion that I did turn on the radio, I heard him speak over the radio and I heard him say that the Omarska camp did not exist. Of course, I felt insulted by what he said because everybody knew about the existence of the Omarska camp, and I remember discussing this with someone. It was strange that he should be denying the existence of the Omarska camp, whereas everybody knew about its existence. But I realised that it meant more to me than others. Had it not been for this Omarska, my husband would probably be still alive, my nephew and many others who perished. At any rate, this was my personal experience of this speech that I heard over the Prijedor Radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Why was it traumatic for you to listen to the radio?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents of radio programmes often involved Muslim extremists, the threat that was coming from Ustashas. I'm now paraphrasing. It was something that I simply couldn't adequately react to. I had to defend myself somehow from these allegations. I wanted to save myself from this kind of environment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, did you try to ascertain the whereabouts of your husband after the Omarska camp closed?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I tried to contact the people who had been in the Omarska camp. I went to the Trnopolje camp after it had been visited by the Banja Luka ICRC and after it was said that family members were allowed to visit detainees there and take food to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me, Doctor. I'm sorry for interrupting you, but I notice the time and it was a new topic I was getting to, so perhaps we can deal with it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stands adjourned until 10.55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, I asked you whether your daughter had been taken for questioning, and you said that she had been taken to the police station. You were answering my question, and you said that your daughter had come to your apartment without her child. And then I interrupted you. Was there anything that you wanted to add in relation to that? How was your daughter eventually taken to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policeman came to fetch her, and they took her by car, and she came back on foot. So there was nothing special in the whole event. One of those policemen I knew, who was embarrassed because we knew each other, and he probably knew me much better than I did know him because, in Prijedor, many more people could know me than I could know them. So there is nothing else to add to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did your daughter tell you what she was questioned about?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly, I know some things. I know that they asked her -- once they asked her about her father and what she thought of her father because of what he had done. And she said: "What had he done? I do not know, but if you tell me, I may know. But I think that my father was an honest man and a citizen of Prijedor. He was a professor, and that he brought me up as a good and honest person, and I'm very grateful to him for that." And after that, they did not comment on this, and this is what she said, what she mentioned about what she had said to them, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, if we can move back to the topic we were dealing with just before we had the break. I asked you whether you had tried to ascertain the whereabouts of your husband after the Omarska camp closed, and you started to answer that you went to Trnopolje. Can you please continue your answer?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw outside many people from Omarska who were transferred here and then later they went home. I don't know in what way but they were released from that camp. And this is where I saw some people who said, "I saw your husband in Trnopolje," and that he had slept with him in a part of a room. Some people told me that on a certain date, he was called. And after that, he did not come back. Professor Zec Adolf, who was a teacher of the physical education in Prijedor, who I used to know, he told me: "Whatever they tell you, they do not know." But he at some point at the end of July, on the 27th or 28th, was called in when the detainees were called in a roll call, and there were buses in which they were taken, nobody knew where to. But afterwards, he never came back. Such stories I heard from Islamovic, Sakib. We were born close by. He was an engineer. He's younger than I am. And he was the director of one department in the Ljubija coal mine. He was also my neighbour where we lived. And he came among the first from Manjaca, the first detainees who went from Omarska to Manjaca. He was among the first to be returned to Banja Luka. And he came to Prijedor through some family relations he had through his wife, who was a Serb. And he came home. He really looked terrible. He had 30 kilos less than he used to have. And he told me: "I tried to register since when he had disappeared. And I thought that it was about eight days prior to the closing up of the Omarska camp. And it could have been the 27th or the 28th of July." After that, wherever I saw someone or I could ask them, I did so, and I mostly asked people who came back from the camps. When they came to Croatia from Manjaca, whichever group arrived, I went in order to see someone and in order to find out, because I did hope that he was alive somewhere, and that if there wasn't this -- the crucial, the 27th or the 28th of July, when he disappeared without coming back. In Zagreb, I met a journalist, Roy Gutman, who at that time still went to Prijedor and to that part of Bosnia. And I asked him if he could, when he went to Prijedor, to ask about my man, about his whereabouts. And as soon as he came back, he told me that the officials in Prijedor told him that he was not there when the takeover of the authority in Prijedor took place, that he had left it prior to that. And I told him that that was not true, that I had a document which, unfortunately, I do not have here but at home in which it says -- and the document was dated the 18th of August, in which it is written that my husband and some other men, some other persons, had been turned to the military court, and that he was no longer under the authority of that particular court. This document was signed by Zivko Dragosavljevic. And I gave this photocopy to Mr. Roy Gutman, and he went for the second time to Prijedor with this document, and he said that he had attended a dinner where all the leaders were present in Prijedor and that he asked about my husband. They told him that on the 27th July, in Omarska, there was no electricity, and some detainees ran away, escaped, and among them also Cehajic. And this is just the most important facts that I know about my asking about my husband. But throughout the war, whenever I saw someone, I asked questions, thinking that my husband might be alive until the end of the war. Then I realised that if he had been somewhere, that he would have come, and this was the end of my trying to find him, to locate him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Banja Luka to find out about your husband's whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was about the 15th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did you travel to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard some information - I do not know whether on the radio or from people - that no passes were necessary to travel. And I decided to take a bus, and I also tried to develop some tactics because people who were going around, who knew, told me what to do. I took a bus from Bosanski Novi to Banja Luka. They told me that that bus was controlled until Prijedor, and then from Prijedor, that it was not controlled. And the one that left Prijedor was controlled from Kozarac onwards. So I took the bus going from Bosanski Novi, and I arrived -- I went to -- I arrived in Banja Luka. And everything was fine, but on our way out, some control came and this man saw my ID, and by the name, he could tell. My name didn't tell him much, but at least my ethnicity. So he asked for my pass for travelling, and I told him that I didn't need -- I thought that I didn't need it. So he let me go. So I arrived in Banja Luka and went to the ICRC. I had with me some business, a business card of the head of the office in Banja Luka who was officially -- who visited me officially in Prijedor, and he gave me his business card. So I thought that this man was still there, so I would show him his business card and mine as well and he would receive me. However, there was no understanding there from the people who were translating for me, and they told me that he was busy and that he couldn't. I was very persistent, so I waited until the afternoon and then I tried through some other people, because there were many translators, interpreters, there. So I told them to give him the business card, and if he couldn't receive me, I would come the following day. Finally, this business card was gone, and this gentleman asked me to come in. And when I entered the room, I saw that this was not the man whose name was written on the business card. And then I apologized and said that I didn't do it on purpose, that I didn't want to cheat him, that this person really had given me the business card. So he said, "That's nothing, okay, I had time. I was free to receive you." He listened to what I had to say, and I asked him, because I thought the IRC was powerful and that they could look for the people who were missing. And I also asked him to take all the data. He did so. And I told him that my husband had been in Omarska, that he wasn't there any more, that he was probably in Manjaca or in some other camp. And that -- I asked him to try to help people. I also said that I had come to ask all the people, not only my husband, but to all the people who needed help in order for them to be treated in a humane way. And at that time, I was really traumatized, and I cried a lot. It was summer. I had a summer dress, and it was all wet of my tears. And that man really was sad, and he tried to comfort me as much as he could at that time. And he took all the personal data and he told me to go, and whatever was in their power, they would do in order to help all the people, and of course my husband as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross later come to Prijedor and telephone you on two occasions?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Twice they telephoned, and they told me -- those at the IRC asked for me. And of course, I interpreted that as some kind of care for me because if they came to Prijedor and asked about me, that I was more secure and that nothing should happen to me in the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you travelled to Banja Luka from Prijedor, did you go along the main Prijedor/Banja Luka Road past Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As you travelled from Prijedor, were you able to see the non-Serb villages along the way?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Kozarac is a village, a small place, which before the war had around 20.000 inhabitants, and the highest percentage were Muslims and a small percentage of other ethnicities. I did saw Kozarac. There are several hamlets actually which belonged to Kozarac, and I saw that everything was destroyed and damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see your -- the villages of Kozarusa and Kamicani?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is all along the way from Banja Luka along the road, so you could see all those villages that you wanted to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What ethnicity of people lived in the villages or lived in the villages of Kozarusa and Kamicani in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly Bosniaks, at least this was how they declared themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the condition of the houses in Kozarusa and Kamicani?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The houses were completely destroyed. It was really terrible to look at them. There might have been one or two that was not completely destroyed, but it was a horrifying sight, as if there was no life at all, only destroyed houses, torn-down houses. This is what you could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you tell me the date that you left Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th of September, 1992. And on the 6th of September, I arrived to Karlovac, in Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Prior to leaving Prijedor, were you ever assaulted? And if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Prior to my departure, because that man, a Serb from Bosanski Novi, told me that he would come to pick me up and that he would take me across the Croatian and Bosnian border. And we made the arrangement. We agreed on the price, 3.000 deutschmarks, to take my sister and me. And he said that I shouldn't take any things with me if I wanted to remain alive because, the less I have, the more securities I would pass. And, of course, I did not take anything. I thought what can I take in a bag if I'm leaving everything else? So I didn't take anything. I had only some money -- I had some money in the bank on my book of my salary, and I went to the bank in order to take that money out, which I meant to leave to my relatives, because my sister's son stayed in Prijedor still, and he did not have any money on him, so he didn't have anything to live on. So that's what I wanted to do, to leave it to this relative of mine in Bosanski Novi, where I would stay overnight in order to wait for my transfer to Croatia. I went to the bank, and there were some guardsmen on the entrance, and they controlled -- they looked at everybody's ID. And this is how my sister and I came. It was our turn, because we were together. And he let her go, but to me, he said: "You are Cehajic's wife, and you are with Dedo Crnalic, a man who was in catering business. You had lamb with your husband at his place." I looked at him, and I said: "Yes, I did go with my husband to many places but I didn't visit Dedo Crnalic's place at all." He looked at me and said: Yes, okay. Okay, go in." And Thank God, if he would have kept me there, I would have passed and stayed on the side. So I entered the bank like many other people. I went to the counter, and I queued, and one of the men came to me and said: "Come out of the queue. Leave the queue," and took me in the back of the bank where there were some offices. I knew of those because I had come many times to the bank. He put me -- took me into an office, and they took my handbag, and they put on the table everything that was in my bag. And they started cursing me, 'the Turkish' -- one of them, 'my Turkish mother,' and such things. At that moment, I do not know whether I was scared, but I could not pull myself together, what was happening in front of all the people who were there. He took me to this room and he closed the door. After him, some other men came. There were altogether five of them, and one young man - he was not very tall - he started cursing my husband. He started mentioning his name. And at some point, he wanted to hit me with his hand. And this taller man who was standing next to me, he put his hand in order to prevent this other man to blow me. So actually, he managed to hit both me and him. So this tall man said -- asked him what he was doing, maybe because he was also hit, and I was hit as well. So I do not know why, but his intention was to protect me, because he put his hand -- he quickly took my handbag, put all the things into it, and also some books that were on the desk, he put in my handbag. He gave the handbag to me and took me out -- quickly out of that room. And I went home after that because I lived close by. I did not know anything. At the moment of that blow, I simply thought at some point that I left my consciousness -- conscience, but I didn't fall down. But I knew for a moment that I did not know anything any more. My head was swollen but nothing hurt, and I actually managed to get to my house. I don't even know how I managed to cross the street, the road. I looked in the -- at myself in the mirror when I came home, and I saw on my face there was a trace of the blow. It was black and blue under my eye. And of course, that was a problem. The following day, when I had to go to Bosanski Novi in order to go to Croatia, it was necessary to do something about this bruise because if someone saw the trace of a blow, then of course they could think that I was someone who needed to be caught again, arrested again, captured again. So when I came home, my sister arrived also. She took the money, and the man in the bank said that he would give her my money without me, and this is how I managed to draw out that money that I needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, these people that were in the office in the bank, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were dressed in various kind of suits. There were several police officers there. Some of them were wearing regular police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: From the 23rd of May until the 5th of September, 1992, did you see any sections of Prijedor city damaged or destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't move around the town of Prijedor very much because after the interview that had taken place in Keraterm, I was told that I should not leave my apartment, that I was under some kind of house arrest. But I also thought that it was not a very good idea for me to leave my apartment because there were very few people who were taken for interrogation and not ended up in a camp. I know this about my daughter, for example, but a number of people were eventually taken to a camp and never returned. So if I had some errands to do, I would leave my apartment but I would remain in the vicinity of the apartment. There is a mosque there -- there used to be a mosque there, and I could see that it was destroyed. There were only remains of the mosque standing. I saw that a part of the Catholic church was also demolished, and at the time I saw it, at the time I passed by, part of the structure was still standing. And after a while, that part was also gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned how you were able to leave Prijedor on the 5th of September, 1992. Did you seek official permission to leave Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sought official permission for my daughter, and I obtained it, a permission for her to leave Prijedor together with my two nieces. Then in August I tried to obtain a permission for myself and wait for the next opportunity to leave. But on that occasion, I was told that I could no longer obtain such a permit, that they were no longer issued. But at any rate, it wasn't so important for me because, even with a permit, I didn't know how I would go about leaving Prijedor. So I no longer went. I no longer tried to obtain this permit. I was trying to find a secret way to leave Prijedor. I didn't want anyone to know that I had left.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Why did you decide to leave Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As days went by, the situation was setting worse. I felt that I should no longer stay there, that I could no longer stay there. Then I started receiving visits of the people who wanted my apartment. My sister had similar visits before me. These people told her that she had to leave, she had to move out of her apartment. She had the same apartment as I had, a four-room apartment, and she had to move out so that they could move in. A soldier eventually came to her apartment. After they had finished with her, they started visiting me in my apartment and telling me I should leave. And two or three days prior to that, a soldier came. They said that they were members of the military police; they were wearing the typical white belts. He said that he heard that I was about to leave my apartment and he expressed his interest in moving in, justifying that with some merits that he had had in the war. I said: "You're a young man. You have enough time. I'm sure you will receive an award for your merits. But this is my apartment. I have spent entire my life and my career living in Prijedor, and this is what I got as a result of that." But that was very usual at the time. People would -- people would choose an apartment for themselves and then exert pressure on those people who lived there. So as I said, two or three days prior to my departure, I had this visit, the visit of this soldier. And I knew that eventually he would force me out of my apartment and I would no longer have a place to live. And this is indeed what happened. So I asked my next-door neighbour to close the window which I had previously opened. I wanted people to think that I was still there. And I switched on the lights, and I asked her to leave the lights on so that I could leave and cross the border because I knew that they would come on the same day. And this is indeed what happened. The same soldier arrived two or three days after my departure, and he moved into my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of this soldier?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. He was a Serb. His name was Gavranovic. His family name was Gavranovic. His name now escapes me, but he was a resident of Prijedor. He lived in a Prijedor neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you sought official permission for your daughter to leave when she left Prijedor in July. Who gave this permission?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were given these permissions in the SUP, the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were there any conditions attached to leaving Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. I had to give up my property. This was a rule which applied to everyone. That was the condition for us to leave the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did your daughter have to sign any documents?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she did. Everybody did. She had to sign personally this document for herself. One of my nieces was above 18, so she signed the document for herself. And this underaged niece, it was her mother who signed on her behalf.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did your daughter ever tell you what was written on the document that she had to sign?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it, too. It was some kind of certificate whereby so-and-so was giving up his or her property for the benefit of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What property belonged to you and your family in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We owned this apartment, a car, a garage, an apartment which was still at the time in construction but which officially belonged to my daughter. I had a family house in Ljubija, some land, some woods. My husband had a family house in Sanski Most which he inherited from his family. And we also had a partly constructed house in Sanski Most. It was not yet finished. It just had a roof on, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In 1992, was the house in Sanski Most that your husband inherited -- what happened to that house, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That house was burned down. Even the debris was removed. Only foundations have remained and a portion of a wall. Everything else is gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The family house in Ljubija in the Prijedor municipality, do you know what happened to that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That family house remained. It was not destroyed, but it was vandalised. It no longer has any door or window frames. It's not suitable for living. It was a very special type of architecture. It was built in 1921, and it was one of the nicest houses in Ljubija. It was built in a typical Austro-Hungarian style, with a carved fence on the terrace and a carved entrance door. It was renovated at one point in time and we tried to renovate it in the traditional style in which it was built. But nobody lived in the house at the time, and it was vandalised.
