utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The partly-constructed house in Sanski Most, do you know what happened to that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is still there. It was not a house that one could live in. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. It's never been finished, and it remained in the same condition as it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In 1992, did you consider yourself well off?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I considered myself well off. We belonged to this group of people who were relatively -- who were doing fine. As a physician, I had a decent salary. But I had to pay tax, of course. Officially, my salary was higher than the -- most of the salaries of people who lived in Prijedor. My husband's salary was not that high. He was a professor at the local high school, and teachers are usually paid less than doctors. But he was a very modest, reasonable man. We had a good life. We had some property from before, and I think that we had a good life, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to move to another topic now. In relation to the fate of your husband, do you know a person by the name of Ermin Strikovic?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Azra Blazevic?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know her. I remember Strikovic. I know him only by his nickname, "Lola." I just remembered. The man is the husband of Azra Blazevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to him about the fate of your husband?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, with Lola. I didn't remember that his name was Erman Strikovic. I know him by his nickname. He was the one who told me about him. He used to be my husband's student, and so did Azra. He told me that my husband was with the group of people who were first taken to Omarska from Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was Erman Strikovic detained in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He told me he had gone together with my husband, that he had been taken together with my husband in this group. He was also at Manjaca, but he survived Manjaca and is currently residing in Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it necessary to redact?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to a person called Mustafa about your husband?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This man is a relative of my husband and lives in Banja Luka. When my husband was in prison in Banja Luka, he was the one who paid him a visit. He took him some essentials that he needed at the time, and he informed me that my husband was in prison. Apparently, it was possible to call from there, and it was possible for the detainees to receive packages. After he left this prison, he called me to say that he was no longer in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Emir Ibrahimbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He told me in Zagreb, because I met with him in Zagreb, that in this prison he been some kind of warden in this prison. I'm not familiar with their ranks. I don't exactly know what he was. And my husband came to Banja Luka to this prison, and when he saw my husband writing a letter addressed to Minka Cehajic, he remembered me. An he said that he had gone to see him. He said that his name was Emir. He didn't want to discuss anything in particular with me. He had to read this letter which had been written by my husband because it was his duty. And he said that more such letters had been written and sent out of the prison. However, those letters never reached me. He said that two or three days passed, and some people came to the prison and said that Croats and Muslims could longer work in prison. So Emir had to leave the prison, so he didn't know exactly when my husband had left prison, this prison. However, a friend of his, a Serb, who was supposed to bring him some documents, told him this friend of yours had left. Emir had probably told him before that he was someone whom he knew from childhood, and that's probably why he said, "this friend of yours."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At some point, did you receive a letter that was written by your husband?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received one letter dated the 9th of June. It was not through the prison authorities that my husband sent this letter. I assume that he had written it in Banja Luka but that he brought it with him in Omarska, that he had this letter in Omarska. And I think that it was there that he met a young man from Prijedor who had approached him and told him that he had seen me in Prijedor going to visit her, that is, my brother. And he said that I was fine. So after a while, perhaps later on that day or some other day, my husband gave him the letter that I still have. And he said: "Please, I know that you will leave this place one day. Please, give this letter to my wife, because I don't think I will ever leave this place." The letter bore my telephone number and the address, and this young man unknown to me, who was also probably frightened because he had been detained in the camp and did not want to be seen in the vicinity of my apartment, he came to see me one day. He knocked on my door, and he simply said: "Here is a letter for you. It was given to me." And this is all he said, and he disappeared. I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you assume that your husband had written it in Banja Luka but that he brought it with him in Omarska, that he had this letter in Omarska. You're referring to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could Dr. Cehajic please be given the letter dated the 9th of June? This will become a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that the letter that you have just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is my husband's handwriting. It was a very special handwriting. You can compare the handwriting in this letter with the handwriting which can be found in the school books and school registers. It's difficult for me from time to time to recognise my own handwriting, but I can definitely always recognise his. He spent so many years as a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you have the original of this letter?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My son has it. He took the letter, and he wanted me to give it to him. He said that it was the only memory that he had of his father. Although the letter was addressed to me, the original is with my son because, as I said, this is the only memory that he has of his father.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you just turn to the second page of the two-page handwritten document. And at the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- there is some text that is missing. Is that also missing on the original?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the original contains this text that is missing here. I think that the word "Muhamed" is there. I haven't recently looked at the letter since I gave it to my son, but I think that it should be there on the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Cehajic, I'm going to ask you to read this letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is an English translation which appears in Roy Gutman's book. We will be seeking an official translation. But if Your Honours wanted to follow it, you can use this document until we have an official translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think in case it's not too problematic, and I would understand this, it would be the best solution for all of us, also, when it comes to problems of handwriting, if you could be so kind and read out this letter, though we know it's difficult for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The title says: "Minka Cehajic." The street is Dzemal Bijedica 16, or the Prijedor hospital, and the telephone is 21771, or 23722, which is my sister's telephone, so he probably thought one or the other. "Banja Luka, the 9th of June, 1992." This is a copy which is not easily legible, but I'll try and do my best. "My dear Minka: I am writing you this letter, though I'm not all certain that you will get it, but I still feel the irresistible need to talk with you in this way."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. May I interrupt you. We are really interested to hear it word by word, and for the interpreters, if you could slow down a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. "Since my departure, since that 23rd of May when they came to our house to get me, I have been living in another world. It seems to me that everything that is happening to me is just an ugly dream, just a nightmare. And I simply cannot understand how something like this is possible. My dear Minka, Amira, and my son: You know how much I love you. You know how much I love you all. And because of this love, I have never done anything, nor would I ever do anything, that would cause you any pain. I know that you know that what they are trying to put on me has nothing to do with me whatsoever. I just keep wondering whom and how much I have offended so that I have to go through all this. But I still believe in justice, and I believe in truth, and I believe that this will all be cleared up. Otherwise, I keep thinking of you constantly, and your faces are always before my eyes. But I have to admit that it is Amir's image that emerges most often before my eyes, and then an occasional tear flows. I know how hard this will be for him, because I know how much he loves me. "I especially ask you, Minka, if you talk to him, please, try to comfort him. Time is passing with dismal slowness, and I can hardly wait for the day when I will be with you again. And you will be sufficient for me for the whole of another world. I would be happiest of all if we could go together far away, where there's no one else. Dear Minka, I'm terribly worried about Sejdo, about Nasa, Biha, and others. I have heard some terrible things, so please, if -- I say so please let me know, if you can, what's happened to them. Safet Mustafa brought me cigarettes, some underwear, and the essentials, and I thank him for that forever. If it hadn't been for that, I would have thought I was completely alone in this world. "I keep wondering, where have all the good friends gone? But so be it. And how's my Benjo doing? Does he ever ask about his grandfather? I missed him so much. Today's the 18th day since I was deprived of my freedom. But to me, it seems like a whole eternity. I don't even know how many times I have been interrogated, and now the investigation is conducted by a judge, Zivko Dragosavljevic. I also asked the lawyer Bereta to attend the interrogations. And I beg you also to engage Sefik Trozic or Emil Kulenovic, whoever wants to. I don't know how much longer they're going to keep me here. If you can, please try and get me some cigarettes somewhere, some soap, toothpaste, two or three pairs of underpants, and an undershirt, a track suit, a shaving set, and some shaving cream. "Don't bother to send me any food, because I cannot eat anyway. But if you can, please send me some ground coffee. As for Amir, tell him to stay with Orhan. And if, God providing, all this settles down one day, then you should go to him. Tell him to just keep studying. And for the hundredth time, tell him that daddy loves him much, much more than he loves himself. I don't even think about myself any more. But he must be an honest and an honourable man. It is inconceivable for me all this that is happening to us. Is it to be that life is so unpredictable and so brutal? "I remember how this time last year we were rejoicing so much over building a house, and now see where we are. I feel so empty. I feel as if I had never been alive. I'm trying to fight it. I'm trying to resist it by remembering everything that was beautiful with you and the children and all those that I love. That's all for this time because I don't have any strength any more. Give my love to all who ask about me. And to you and the children, I love you very, very much."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stands adjourned until 12.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. The Prosecutor may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Cehajic, when did you receive the letter that was written by your husband?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been August. Most probably after the closing up of the camp. When that young man came out, he didn't -- well, probably in August, in the second half of August, some time before my departure. I just remembered that I did not know about this letter at the moment I had left to Banja Luka, so it must have been towards the end of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said earlier that Sakib Islamovic, a detainee in Omarska camp, told you that he saw your husband in Omarska up until the end of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's Sakib Islamovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also said earlier that you asked questions throughout the war, trying to find out about your husband, and at the end of the war, you stopped trying to find him because, had he been alive, he would have come to you.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Have you attended any of the exhumations that have been conducted in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was present at some. In Sanski Most, they exhumed, and they were brought to Sanski Most and exposed in the halls there. And I went every time, hoping that I might recognise and find my husband there. And this is what I did. I went to see those people that were brought there. Every time I went there, I knew that there was nothing to recognise him, that that was impossible. But still I had a need to go every time for this identification. And every time, I went through a terrible thing. It was very difficult for me, but I had to do it for my husband. I had to go and see. But it wasn't possible to recognise him, and I only hope -- the DNA, we did give that for the analysis, the DNA, so if that might make it possible to find him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Cehajic, I have no further questions for you. If you could just wait there for one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you want me to tender the exhibits now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The first document which was referred to yesterday, which was Prosecution -- which was marked P650 in the Rule 65 ter exhibit list, dated the 10th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was already admitted as S49.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is admitted as S49.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The next document today was -- Your Honour, Ms. Karper, the case manager, has it as S48.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. I'm already one step further. 465, I think this will be the next now, the former 465.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, that will be S49.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. I had already marked this provisionally S49.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the letter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: S49B, because we have it only in B/C/S. But I don't think a translation is necessary. We have it on the transcript. Objections from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, same as before, on the same grounds, for the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I take it, just for the record, and so this is admitted as S49B.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a draft summary translation just of the heading and of the signature block.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. We already have the most important points brought into -- tendered into evidence by the transcript and by the annotations and the remarks by Dr. Cehajic. And I think this forms at the end of the day one unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But I appreciate if you later on give this as S49A as a translation in part to the registry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The registry and the parties have been provided with copies already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Fine. Then it's S49A, this translation in part.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the letter dated the 9th of June, 1992, could be marked S50, letter written by Muhamed Cehajic to Minka Cehajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: S50. Could we here agree -- I'm hesitant to use that, what we have here as a part of a book, as a formal translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The Prosecution will be requesting an official translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In both languages, please, in English and French, please. Then this document, the letter, objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is then admitted into evidence as S50B. I wonder, because I don't know whether the Defence will come back to this, this would be, of course, a surprise, but before the Judges come back to other documents offered in this context, what about the former 65 ter Document 625?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I don't seek to tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you want to leave it for the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then we have, in addition, another document offered until now but not yet tendered. It is 65 ter Document Number 476.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't seek to tender that document at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it will be -- the Defence may be prepared that both documents will be tendered by the Judges. So I understand this was the end of the examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we may start with the cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Cehajic, my name is John Ostojic, and I'll be asking you questions here this afternoon. Okay? Doctor, initially, I'd like to ask you some general questions with respect to the testimony that you gave, and if you can be so kind enough to help clarify some issues that I continue to have questions on. Can you help us with that, please?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever attend a meeting of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever attend a meeting of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I understand that you gave a statement to the OTP in 1997 in connection with that which you've experienced tragically in Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that during the period of 1990 through 1992, April of 1992, that you personally, Doctor, did not notice any animosity between the politicians in the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice. I thought that they were in a coalition and that they were dividing the power, so I did not notice any animosities. My husband did not talk about this, and I wanted to exclude myself, to be out of it, because in the past, I had been an active member as a politician, an amateur, and at that time I didn't want to get involved at all. And to go in depth and to analyse, I turned to myself. I wanted to see who I am and what -- from what I am and how I could think then. It was really stressful for me also because I had been brought up at different times. And when this multiparty system came, it was a change for me, and I wanted to really gather whatever was good in myself and then start thinking about the new society that I had to live in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may ask you, Doctor, prior to April of 1992, were you familiar with whether or not there was an inter-party agreement between the SDS and SDA?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, yes, because they have divided the powers. There was this agreement, as much as I know about it. But I do not know of any other agreements. I only know that in February 1992, the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor was formed, the Serbian Municipal Assembly. But I was not interested in that. And my husband did not talk about it. He did not talk about it as something that could bring some changes or some bad things. And I, myself, was -- wanted to exclude myself from this kind of thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would it fair, from February 1992 through approximately April 30th, 1992, to say that your husband, the late Mr. Cehajic, that he continued to negotiate and discuss and meet with members of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot either confirm or say no, because I do not know. Of course, he went to work. He worked, and I do not know any details about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me, if I may, direct your attention to another topic that we've discussed here at the trial, without your presence at times. That's the issue of mobilisation. Doctor, do you know in Prijedor or in Bosnia in 1991 how many mobilisation call-ups were there?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not give you an answer as far as the numbers are concerned because I cannot talk about what I do not know. Because if I do not know, then that's not the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that very much, as does everyone else in this room. So is it fair to say that you don't know whether there was one, two, or more than two mobilisation call-ups in the area in 1991? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was simply not interested in that, and I did not register something like that in my head at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Directing your attention, if we may, to approximately April 30th, 1992, which is I believe the time-line that the parties may ultimately agree as the day of the takeover of Prijedor by the Serbs. With respect to that date, you testified that you were awakened in your home by a friend who called you and that then you woke up your husband and shared the news with him. Correct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll direct her.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, if I may --

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Subsequent to that discussion -- the telephone call with your friend and discussion with your husband, can you tell us whether or not your husband proceeded to go to the radio station and give an announcement at all?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't go to the radio station, but he stayed at home. As I said, he was given a decision that he was on an annual leave, that he was actually taken from his position. And during that day, I was told - and because I was working I didn't listen to the radio because in the hospital I couldn't do that - I heard that he was invited to come to the radio station and that he said something there. But I cannot even paraphrase the content of what he said because I didn't think it was anything important at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All right. And thank you for the correction. Is it fair to say that it's your understanding that on April 30th, your husband, Mr. Cehajic, was invited to come to the radio station, and that he, in fact, did come to the radio station and was asked questions or gave a statement on the radio?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be, but I cannot state that because I do not know. At that time, I did not check it with him because if he was, he was there, but this is not my truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, Doctor, at any time check that with your husband subsequent to April 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, because from the 30th of April to the 23rd of May, he was at home. And I used to go to work. I would come back, and then we would discuss our things. But we tried to avoid the reality, so we did not talk much about it. And I had a feeling, and now I have a feeling, that he wanted to comfort me, that nothing was terrible, or at least he thought it wasn't. So even there was a fear, but we did not talk about it. He did not tell me anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I understand that, Doctor. Thank you for those comments. Is it fair to say to this day that you don't know what it is, if anything, that your husband may have said on that radio programme on or about April 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he said. I did hear something, that they had invited him, and that they at the beginning were disturbing father-in-law and that he probably left the flat at some point. I do know that, and that was something that hurt me because why to look for him at my daughter's house or at her father-in-law's house? But the content, what he had to talk about, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. If I may turn also to that date, you mentioned that you heard an announcement on the radio. And when asked, on page 67 of yesterday's transcript, line 22, I believe, you stated upon questioning by the Office of the Prosecutor that at this point you cannot recall the contents of that announcement in detail. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But roughly speaking, I could say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll give you that opportunity. What I'd like to know, though, is that if you remember whether or not the speaker who gave the announcement, whether or not it was a male or female speaker?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a woman, because in all that fear, I do not know and I do not want to talk about this announcement because I did not register its content. But I know that the power was -- the authority was taken over without any shooting. I thought it was a female voice in that announcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And to this day, do you know who that voice belongs to, who the person is that made that announcement? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be honest. I know what then it was but I don't remember. It is something that I have heard from others. I know Ganic Alija has read the announcement, that Dr. Stakic had said something beforehand, but I didn't hear it. This is what I want to say. What I'm talking about today is a different thing. I cannot testify because this is not what I had heard then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And Doctor, that's exactly -- we're asking only for the testimony and only the recollections that you personally have. And as you have in your statement and as you have in the questioning by the Office of the Prosecutor, if you would be kind enough to indicate for us when it is something that would be considered hearsay or something that you heard from others. I'm particularly only interested in that which you've heard and that which you've experienced.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally heard, as far as I remember now, that that was a speaker, someone of the speakers. And what else there is, I didn't even talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that it was that same voice that you heard repeatedly, although you resisted from listening to the radio for a number of reasons, your personal convictions and disappointment in the situation, as well as the fact that there was a lack of electricity and power in Prijedor subsequent to April 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it is. And I had said that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You also testified, I believe yesterday, that the document that your husband, Mr. Cehajic, received on April 30th, 1992 regarding his discharge, for lack of a better term, you did not review it or you did not see that document. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But to this day, is it fair to say that you don't know who signed it? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, since I didn't see the document, I didn't see the signature either. I never said anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, and I'm not suggesting, Doctor, that you did. I was just merely trying to inquire as to whether you learned from others who may have signed it and in what capacity they signed it. So if I may, and I know they may seem trivial questions for you, and I apologise; I'm trying to speed it up as much as possible. Is it fair to say that you don't know who signed that document that we're referencing, the letter that your husband received on or about April 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He got it while I was at work on the 30th of April, and he told me: "This is what I got. I have been replaced. I'm on leave now." I didn't check anything. I didn't pay much attention to it so I didn't see who signed the document. I didn't know it would turn out to be this important. After a while, when these people came to the house to get these things, they took this document as well. If it had stayed in the house longer, I would have probably looked at it again, but I didn't. So all I know is what actually my husband had told me at this moment. He had no reason to lie to me or to tell me anything that would not be true. He did not say who signed the document. He just said that Dr. Stakic was appointed to such and such position, but we didn't discuss the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No one's making that suggestion at all, Doctor. With respect to the period of April 30th, 1992 through May 23rd, 1992, can you tell us generally, other than going to work, what were some of the activities that you and your husband engaged in? Other than you going to work, what did your husband do during that time period?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was at home. He was reading. I know that he told me that he had gone out a couple of times for a walk in the vicinity of our house before I arrived. When I came home, we spent the time together. Whenever we had free time, we always enjoyed spending it together. The two of us were enough to one another. We did not discuss politics or what was going on, because both of us could clearly see what the situation was and were waiting to see what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if your husband engaged in any or participated in any meetings with members of the SDS at that time, again, April 30th through May 23rd, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he did, but again, this is just my opinion, and probably the best answer would be that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fair. Do you know if during that time period April 30th through May 23rd, 1992, your husband had or held any meetings with members of the Municipal Assembly or the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if at that time, April 30th through May 23rd, 1992, your husband held or attended any meetings with the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if during that time period your husband had any meetings with Mirza Mujadzic, who is the president or identified previously, I believe, by yourself - and correct me if I am wrong - as the president of the SDA in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was at home, no. But during those eight hours that I would spend at work or when I was on duty, and therefore, 24 hours absent from my home, I don't know. But when I was present at home, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all we're trying to find out, is what you knew and what you observed. Thank you, Doctor. Is it -- strike that. Do you know if during the period of April 30th through May 23rd, 1992, your husband was ever arrested or detained?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not. Until the 23rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. And I appreciate that. So it's fair to say from April 30th up until May 22nd, 1992, your husband was never detained or arrested. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we know, as you shared with us, on May 23rd, your husband was arrested for the first time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may direct a comment or a question, I should say, I apologise, to the Court. On line 24, there seems to be no answer, Your Honour, to the question that commenced on line 21. So I'm not sure if I should restate the question, just so that we have a record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the witness nodded to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't see that. I was looking at my notes. If I may ask that question again, Your Honour, to get a verbal response. May I, Your Honour? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm going to ask you a question that you've already probably answered, but just for our clarification, is it fair to say, from April 30th up until May 22nd, 1992, your husband was never detained or arrested? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may just return to an issue that we briefly discussed. We talked about mobilisation, if you remember, earlier this afternoon or several minutes ago. And I recognise that you don't know how many mobilisations there may have been in 1991. Do you know, Doctor, what the position was of your husband in 1991 during the mobilisation with respect to whether or not Bosnian Muslims should participate in the call-up for mobilisation during the war against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share that with us, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His position was that one should not go to fight war in Croatia because our state was Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Croatia was a different state. And he thought that we should not go -- we or anybody else, for that matter, should not go to Croatia to fight a war there. I know that this was his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was that his position as a member of the SDA or as the president of the Municipal Assembly of the municipality of Prijedor in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his position was as a member of the SDA. I never attended their meetings. But his personal conviction was that we should not go to Croatia to fight a war there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if during the war in Croatia your husband expressed his view that the Muslims and Croatians only should not join the war in Croatia, and he expressed this view continuously?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't think that. He was of the opinion that no one should go to war. As far as I know, this is not -- this was not his view.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Also tell us if this was his view or not: Did your husband tell the non-Serbs not to fight against the Croats? Was that ever the view of your husband?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot confirm that. I know that it was his position that no one should go to war in Croatia, be it a Croat, a Serb, or a Muslim. I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At that time, you mentioned that -- or at that time in 1991, was Bosnia-Herzegovina still a part of what's known as the former Yugoslavia? Were they still part of that federation?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As a result of a referendum which was held in March - I don't remember the exact date, it could have been the 27th of March - it became an independent state; that is, the majority of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina had expressed already their wish to become independent, as was the case with other republics of the former Yugoslavia. As for the recognition, well, we know when it happened, the recognition by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My question, Doctor, if I may, and I apologise if I was convoluted in the questions or unclear, the issue that you're talking about, the independence of Bosnia, occurred in 1992, did it not? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992. You asked me about 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. And it was my fault, and I apologise for that. With respect to 1991 and the mobilisation issue in particular, I think in one of your answers you shared with us the sentiments of your husband, but in part of your answer, I thought - and I may have been mistaken, and you can help clarify that - you are saying that Bosnia is a separate state and they shouldn't go for that reason. Regardless of that, at that time, in 1991, do you agree with me that Bosnia was still part of the federation known as former Yugoslavia, or currently known as former Yugoslavia? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The former Yugoslavia, yes, but it was a federal state. The former Yugoslavia was made of several federal states: There was a state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then a federal state, the former Yugoslavia. If that is what you had in mind, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the former Yugoslavia still continued to have a military; do you know? Or if you don't, you can share with us that you don't.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that it did, even after 1992. After the referendum, and after all these events, the Yugoslav People's Army was still in Bosnia. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In 1991, would it be fair to identify respectfully the politicians in the Prijedor municipality as local politicians as opposed to federal politicians or republic politicians or national politicians?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't describe it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How would you describe the local politicians who were representatives and members of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see what you mean, what kind of definition you have in mind. I don't understand your question, I'm afraid. I didn't have any specific definition for them, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fair. I'm not looking necessarily for a definition, but really a description from your perspective as being the wife of the former president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. And respectfully, I don't want to minimise what your husband has done or the other politicians in Prijedor, but I must ask you this question: Was the position of president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor a local political position?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I know the answer to that question. It was probably a local one, but I don't know. I don't have an answer. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any political offices that fell below the office of the representatives of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There must have been, I'm sure. I'm sure that there was a hierarchy, as it is customary within a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you know what the hierarchy was going up instead of going down from the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the hierarchy went from Prijedor through Banja Luka all the way up to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if you know, where did that hierarchy proceed after Sarajevo in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure. I know what the former system was. Well, if we're talking about the former state, the former Yugoslavia, then the end of this hierarchy would be in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to the organs that were in the Prijedor municipality, were there some republic or federal institutions in Prijedor in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where, in Prijedor? I'm sorry, I missed the beginning. Are you referring to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any federal governmental institutions that were in the Prijedor municipality in 1991/1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think I already answered this in response to your previous question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise if you had. Let me change the subject, if I may, a little bit. You worked at the hospital, or as you call it, the balisi [phoen] in Prijedor for many years. Can you tell me the structure of that hospital? Was it affiliated or connected to other institutions within and outside the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. The hospital was part of a larger medical institution, Dr. Mladen Stojanovic Clinic, which consisted of several departments and my hospital was one such department. There was a pharmacy, and then a local health centre in Prijedor, the institute for occupational medicine in Prijedor, the health centre in Sanski Most and the health centre in Bosanski Novi. And also, a unit, administrative unit, in Prijedor, which all made up a whole which was called Dr. Mladen Stojanovic medical institution which was, in turn, part of an even larger organisation, SOUR, as we called it at that time, which was an umbrella organisation comprising all medical institutions in Prijedor. And our hospital was part of that larger organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The municipalities of Bosanski Novi and Sanski Most, are they separate and distinct from the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Politically speaking, yes, they were separate, but the medical institutions were connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you know, and I know that you were the -- one of the directors at the hospital for a period of time but I don't know for sure if you would know the answer to this question: Do you know if during that time period what, if any, influence the politicians or the people from the municipality of Sanski Most and Bosanski Novi had on the institution of the hospital or the clinics at which you served?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, it did not have any significant influence. We constituted a medical organisation which did not -- which was not exposed to any such influence, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Doctor, if there were any other areas which also had these associations between various municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I know about our work organisation, and I told you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us, if I can call it an "association," can you tell us how long these associations between the various municipalities were in existence prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of health, I don't know what year it was - I don't remember - but I know that roughly 350.000 residents were under the jurisdiction of this medical institution which had its seat in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman by the name of Risto Banovic?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He was one of the managers. He was actually the manager of this work organisation, this association, at the time I was manager at my hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So was he the manager or the director, or can we use the terms interchangeably?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a director. "Manager" is a more general term. He was the director of this work organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not Mr. Banovic in 1992 was discharged and relieved from his duties as director?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was. He told me on -- over the telephone, when I asked him whether anyone else can receive my salary on my behalf, he said that he no longer had this function and that he was no longer in a position to approve this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us, if you recall, the date of that telephone conversation or the approximate month and year that it may have occurred?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe in the month of June. In the course of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You are talking about June of 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where was Mr. Banovic located in approximately June of 1992? Where was his office, home, position?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I dialed the number of this working organisation -- work organisation, so he was probably still at his duty station where he worked before, just that he was no longer the director.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And where was that, ma'am? Was that in the municipality of Prijedor or a different municipality?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the municipality of Prijedor in the Urije neighbourhood, near the new hospital where there was an administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, if you know, what the ethnic background is of Mr. Risto Banovic, the person we are discussing here?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time inquire of Mr. Banovic why he got discharged?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. But he could probably -- the case was probably that he could no longer be trusted. He could go on working, but he could no longer be a director. Unlike myself, who was not able either to work or be a director. He was a Serb. He was allowed to continue working, but he could no longer be a director. In any society, including the communist system, people who were trusted or considered to be suitable were on managing positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may now switch to a separate issue, and that was the interrogation that you had to regrettably undergo on or about June 11th, 1992, according to my notes. May I ask some questions about that interrogation, please?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was on the 11th. The 11th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. I have that. Just briefly, and I don't want to recollect all of that, because I know obviously it has left an impact, tragic, on you, so if you can just patronise me for a moment and let me just ask a couple questions on this issue. You mentioned that the interrogator himself seemed to be unorganised and didn't really know what he was asking you or what information he wanted to obtain from you. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less, because he didn't ask any specific questions. And I spent quite some time there with him. But he never asked any significant question as to the reasons of my being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So would it be fair to conclude, and you help us with this, if you can, that the questions were not in any way, shape, or form scripted?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had been prepared in advance, but he didn't ask any concrete, specific questions. I am simply unable to convey to you what it was that he wanted from me, and I don't know to this very date. But obviously, he knew everything about me, so one can perhaps argue that he had been prepared. He knew that I had been a member of the League of Communists, that I had been a member of the local committee of the party. He knew about my family, about my brother, what kind of function he had. He knew all about that. There's six of us in my family, and out of six of us, five have university degrees. My brothers, they all held high, managing positions. My brother was an economist, a financial director of the mines throughout that period of time. I have another brother who is an engineer. My sister is also highly educated. And he knew all about that. He even knew about my father, what he had done during the Second World War, that he supported Partisans. So he was well aware of all this, and he intimated this knowledge to me. And in a way, I felt that he wanted to facilitate things for me at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In any event, despite the fact that he may have known a lot about it, is it fair to say that the questions that he asked, according to what you felt, were not concrete, were not precise, and seemed to have no bearing whatsoever on the purpose for which they detained you and brought you for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my feeling was that there was no specific reason that I had been brought there. They obviously didn't have anything to ask and didn't have anything against me, anything on the basis of which they could have accused me of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may just turn briefly to another issue, and that is you state that in August of 1992, you met Simo Miskovic with a friend of yours who was at one time, according to your testimony, the president of the SDS. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Miskovic, during that one conversation that you inquired about your husband with your friend, did he or did he not tell you at that time that, "We do not have any control over this any more"?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what he said. When he said "we," I understood him to mean the SDS, because he had some kind of function at the SDS. Whether I accepted his answer and trusted him is another matter, but those were his words. That's the way he put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to, if I may, turn to another issue, and that is, you mentioned that in August of 1992, you used your telephone to call the IRC. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't call them; I was in Banja Luka. I visited Banja Luka in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this: In May and June of 1992, is it fair to say that you used your telephone and that it was operating?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It caused me a lot of problems because of various forms of harassment. So at one point in time, I had to disconnect it in order not to be disturbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in July, did your phone also work? Because I think you shared with us at one point that your daughter may have called in connection with your grandchild. Is it fair to say that your phone was operating in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. My phone was operating all the time. It is true that from time to time, the lines would be down with Banja Luka, for instance. But when the line was functioning, my telephone was operating as well. I talked to a friend of mine who was in Belgrade, who had gone to school with me in Zagreb. Sonja Badham [phoen] is her name. She was a journalist at the time. And I wanted her to get in touch with my son and tell him that I was alive. Now, I remember that sometime before that, we had celebrated the anniversary of the high school prom, the 30th anniversary of the high school prom, and I had this business card of hers, and I contacted her and my son was able to learn that I was alive. I'm telling you this because I was not cut off. I had my telephone operating at house.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps I shall just ask the more direct question, and that's what I was getting to: My point was that in fact your telephone was operating during the entire period of time, specifically, the period from April 30th, 1992, up to and including September 5th, 1992, when you departed Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except from occasional disruptions, and when I, myself, disconnected the phone when they harassed me. Yes, from time to time, the line was disrupted, but I don't think that they had done it on purpose, though it's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure, and anything is possible. I'll agree with you there. To the best that you can recall, were these interruptions intermittent and inconsistent and lasted for only short periods of time?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time, we would have the connection with Banja Luka but not with Sanski Most. But I was in the same situation as anyone else. The line would be disrupted maybe for one day or two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about the electricity? Did you have access and was the electricity operating for the entire period of time, from April 30th, 1992, through September 5th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were very often without electricity. There was a period of time when I was not able to make myself a cup of tea or coffee, and I didn't dare leave the apartment. There was a longer period of time without electricity, and I tried to make some fire on the balcony to boil the water for tea. But in view of everything else, it was a marginal thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Doctor, the reason as to why there was lack of electricity or lack of power in the Prijedor municipality during that time period, April 30th, 1992 through September 5th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the reason. Nobody told me, nor did I inquire. I know that Serbs living in my building would go to other places where it was possible to either make fire or cook something, and they would bring this food from there, which is something that for me was not possible to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the Serbs who were living in your building, having had to go to other places to either make fire or cook something, also meant that there was lack of electricity for them in their apartments as well? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It would be impossible to cut the electricity only for my household. There were about ten apartments in this building. They couldn't disconnect my apartment only.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, Doctor, whether or not there were any electrical disruptions or interruptions prior to April of 1992 in the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We had very rare disruptions, an insignificant number of them. I mean, it's not something that I observed as being a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just have a few more questions. I'm hoping to be able to wrap up. Do you know of an incident that has been coined, at least in my mind, in this Chamber, of an incident called the Hambarine incident that took place on or about May 22nd, 1992? Are you familiar with that incident?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it fair to say, Doctor, and just so that I establish my time line and our time line for the Defence here, that in fact your husband was arrested after the incident occurred on Hambarine on May 22nd, 1992? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The arrest of my husband took place when there was -- the Hambarine was attacked on the 23rd at 12.00, when there was this ultimatum. And then I said at half past 3.00, he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't want to split hairs with you, and thank you for your patience here today. My point is a little different. There was an incident that occurred at a checkpoint in Hambarine on or about May 22nd. As a result of that incident, there was what has been also called an attack on the area of Hambarine. So I respectfully understand and accept your testimony wholeheartedly as to the timing of your husband's arrest vis-a-vis the attack on Hambarine. My question, although slightly different, is: Do you know whether or not your husband was arrested before or after the incident that occurred in Hambarine on May 22nd, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has already sustained that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair, Doctor to state --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course you may, if you want.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he asked me about this incident, I didn't even mention it in my statement, but I know incidentally because it is connected with it. I was on duty on the 22nd of May, and I was at the hospital, and I came to the surgery where I was present at an event where some reporters, journalists from Radio Prijedor, were shooting on a videocassette a conversation with people who were in the vehicle that later took place as an incident at Hambarine. I thought that, as a witness, something would happen to me. I was scared that night because I heard when this young man had said -- actually, two young men were in the surgery who were slightly hurt, and the third was also hurt much more. I didn't see him. They said he had gone to Banja Luka. These two young men said that -- I did hear that, and I can witness if there was this videocassette that we could see. I heard when he said, "We went to Hambarine, we passed the guards, and they told us to stop. The driver who had -- who was hurt stopped. And at some point, he suddenly started, and they started shooting at us." This is what I had heard, this statement. And there was no reason that my husband would have been taken or that he would have been arrested for that. When I heard that, I was scared because I knew that I was a live witness of that, and later on people were talking about that all these three young men were hurt, and I saw two of them who were not hurt at all. And I really felt this as a necessity to say something about it because you had asked me. I didn't think it was necessary to testify on this, but since you have asked me, this is what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. The Defence may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On line 8, page 7 -- on line 8, page 78 of your testimony here just moments ago, you state: "I didn't even mention it in my statement." Can you tell me which statement you're referring to in which you didn't mention this what you just described to us?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a statement -- I don't know how many years ago, in what year. Maybe it is present here. Maybe 1997. Somebody asked me officially. This is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if in that statement of 1997, whether you mentioned the incident at Hambarine at all?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if in that statement of 1997, you mention anyone by the name of Mr. Aliskovic?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, maybe I did, if they had asked me about the 23rd of May. Because on the radio, there was this ultimatum that a policeman named Aliskovic ought to be handed over or Hambarine would be attacked. This is how it was. And on that day, on the 23rd, at 12.00, because they probably had not handed over this man, there was this attack on Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And finally, if I may ask you, with respect to Dr. Stakic, you have had no personal contact with him. Would that be a fair characterisation?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This could be said. He also knows that it was not either as friends or as enemies. He was a colleague that I knew, and I did not know much about him. I wasn't even interested because the situation was not such as if I ought to know about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Finally, is it also fair that you had no professional contact with Dr. Stakic as well during any period of time, so no personal contact as well as no professional contact. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible because I worked -- I was very often on duty at hospital, and maybe he sent a child who I actually received. I don't remember. Maybe we were in some contact in such a way, because there were -- he worked in Omarska. He checked on adults and on children. He may have sent some child to the hospital. He might have referred a child. This was what the professional connection was. We may have been at some conferences together where we gave speeches, because this is what physicians and doctors do. This is where we might have seen each other. But this was not such an important thing to be mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But Doctor, as far as you know, sitting here today, based on the recollection you have today, you don't have any recollection of ever interacting professionally with Dr. Stakic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe he remembers. I don't remember. But he -- if he could remind me, maybe I would remember myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With your approval, and the Court's, I do have a couple follow-up questions if you don't mind, although I indicated it might be my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, may I ask you just a couple more questions. Thank you. Doctor, just going back briefly to your tenure in the hospital, who provided the payments and how was the hospital financed in 1991 and prior?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the fund of the health protection. Through the fund, we all received our salaries. It was actually allocated to different basic organisations. So for associated labour, the head office was in Banja Luka, but this was a branch office in Prijedor, and this is how the administration of the health organisation was managed in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who, if you know, contributed the funds for the operation of the health system and your hospital in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went from our personal salaries, and it was collected in the fund and it was later allocated on the basis of some contracts which were made annually. I was very often present when these agreements were made in order to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But who gives you the money which you would decide to distribute to the various parts and personnel at the hospitals? Where do you get the money from?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said from the fund, and then from the fund to the bank, and then we allocated the money within our individual basic organisations of the so-called associated labour. Maybe I did not understand your question properly. But if you want to know anything else, I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It was probably a poor question, and let me just try one last time. And if I don't understand it or if you don't, then I'll move on to something else. The fund that holds the money, who puts the money in that fund? Where does that money come from? Does it come from a municipal assembly of any sort? Does it come from more than one municipal assembly? Does it come from a republic? Does it come from a federal government, or does it come from all portions of those four, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you. The main source were the personal salaries, regardless of which institution, health system or everywhere. It was taken from each person. It went to the fund, so these were the contributions. It was named differently. At some point, it was a fund or a health insurance. And according to that, the main part would come from that source. There were also some individual parts. We would be given money from different companies, from the coal mine, from the fabrika, and the municipality was the one who actually took care of all that. But these were not the permanent sources. It may have been just temporary sources. Whether the municipality contributed, I don't know. Yes, they probably did, because there was this compulsory insurance for the socially deprived persons, but these were all very small amounts. And the largest amount came from the fund of the health system or health insurance fund. I hope I have answered correctly, sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You have. Thank you, Doctor. Where is the seat of this fund?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Prijedor was a branch office, and we used to say that the main office was in Banja Luka where all the money came to. And then everything was later on distributed to different municipalities and individual health organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, thank you very much. I have no further questions

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Are there any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have two matters. I don't know -- I think it will take longer than two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We would have I think for additional five minutes. Would the interpreters, in the interest of the witness, be prepared that we proceed 12 minutes sharp? I see nodding. Okay. Let's try to be short.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Cehajic, in cross-examination, you were asked questions about your husband's media statements. To your knowledge, did your husband ever give any advice or did he have a position regarding resistance or armed resistance to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know. I think that he didn't, but I do not know. I do not know of any such statements that he would have made.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The other area you were questioned about, or another area, you were asked about your phone being in operation between the time 30th of April until you left Prijedor. You answered that the phone -- you disconnected the phone a number of times because it caused you a lot of problems because of various forms of harassment. Can you explain to the Court --

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- what you meant by "various forms of harassment"?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you one thing that is probably the most crucial one, but there were constant harassment. There was one thing that disturbed me a lot. There was a telephone call from Prijedor. A telephone rang one day. And a person said, "I'm Mira Kuruzovic." Mira Kuruzovic was, I understood, the wife of Mr. Kuruzovic, who was the head of the camp at Trnopolje. And she told me: "You need to give me deutschmark." And I asked, "Why do I need to give you deutschmark?" She said, "Because you owe me from many years ago when we travelled to Poland." And she said the following: "You were the last. We sat in the first seats. You sat in the first seats, and I sat on the last one. And I paid for the customs duty and you didn't. And this is why you have to give me the money." And I answered -- I did know Mira. She was from Prijedor. She even used [as interpreted] in the health system. I said "Mira, I don't have any deutschmark." And she said, "I want you to send me or leave it in the cashiers in a shop of a man -- salesman called Huran [phoen]. There's a man who works there. You bring it there and leave it." And I said I didn't have any money. But she kept calling me. And then at once, I told her that I had some money in the bank, and I wasn't even aware how much. And I said: "Mira, if you want, I shall go to the bank and draw that money, but I don't have deutschmark." She said she didn't want the local money, she wanted deutschmark. And she also said that that was not enough. And of course, I had to disconnect my telephone because of such harassment. And one day, I asked my neighbour to help me because he had always been very kind to me. And at that time, for me, it was enough that somebody just said "hello" to me because it was a different time. And he told me: "Okay, I will try to help you." And I really did see that he meant it. And at some point, he remembered that she was the wife of Slobodan Kuruzovic and that I was the wife of Muhamed Cehajic and that something could be attributed to you because this will be by telephone. But I shall see what can be done. He mentioned the Crisis Staff, and he said he would see what he could do. So it was on the stairway when he was just passing by me. And really, afterwards, this woman did not call any more, and this is how all my troubles stopped and ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions on that. Did you, in fact, buy any goods in Poland which required you to pay customs?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't buy anything. We went because of an excursion, the professors of the high school, and they took their wives with them and some friends. I didn't buy anything, and neither did I have to pay the customs duty. Whatever I had seen there, I had at home, so I didn't buy anything and I didn't have to pay any customs duty. It was such an unimportant moment that I did not consider would be the reason for someone to ask me and harass me by asking money for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Before your neighbour was able to contact the people he contacted in order for these phone calls to be stopped, on approximately how many occasions did Mira Kuruzovic, the wife of Slobodan Kuruzovic, telephone you?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it happened several times, many times. I did not count, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. but I'm sure quite a number of times that she had -- that she called me because she kept asking, "You still don't have the money. You still haven't collected my money." Had I had the money at that point, I probably would have given it to her. The money that I later paid for my departure, it was not with me at the time. It was at my family house in Ljubija. And only later I managed to get that money. Had I had it at that point, I probably would have given it to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. I have to interrupt now. I thought there would be only two questions by the OTP put forward, but now it doesn't make any sense. We have to answer the questions from the Judges. And would it be possible for you to come back tomorrow morning at 9.00, because -- I know it's really difficult, but we have to consider the interest not only of the interpreters but also there is another case scheduled starting in 20 minutes from now. And therefore, I have to apologise, but we really have to come back to the one or other question still open, because your statement is really of utmost importance for all of us, and we won't forget to ask you the remaining questions. You gave numerous insights today, and I hope this will continue tomorrow. Thank you. The Court stands adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00.
